newsitem.title: USA: RJR denounces FTC action against Joe Camel.
newsitem.headline: RJR denounces FTC action against Joe Camel.

text.p: RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp unit R.J. Reynold Tobacco Co on Wednesday denounced the U.S. Federal Trade Commission's vote to seek a court order barring it from using its "Joe Camel" symbol in ads accessible to children, saying there was "no factual basis" for such a lawsuit.

"Today's vote by the Federal Trade Commmission to issue a complaint against Joe Camel is unprecedented, unfounded and unwarranted. There is absolutely no precedent in FTC history for such a tortured application of the law," the company said in a statement.

The tobacco company issued its fiery protest after the FTC voted 3-2 to seek the order, alleging the Joe Camel campaign was "successful in appealing to many children and adolescents under 18" and induced many to begin and continue smoking to the detriment of their health."
"There is no factual basis on which to found this suit," Reynolds said, adding, "Joe Camel has become the government's scapegoat for issues our society has been unable to resolve.
"That is not enough to win a lawsuit. We will vigorously defend this complaint, and we fully expect to prevail," the company said.
The FTC, in announcing the vote, said its complaint would be heard before an administrative law judge.

The regulatory agency added it would seek to have Reynolds conduct a public education campaign discouraging young people from smoking and could consider other penalties against the company after a trial of the case was concluded.

"The real loser today is the American public," said Charles A. Blixt, Reynolds senior vice president and general counsel, who warned that other businesses such as the music and alcoholic beverage industries could also find themselves jeopardized by FTC theory.

"The penalties sought by the Commission represent an astonishing and unprecedented use of government authority that would exceed both legal precedent and any reasonable interpretation of the FTC's authority," Reynolds said.
It added that such penalties would force Reynolds to incur a burden "that would not be borne by competitors with much larger shares of market among underage smokers."
"The FTC cannot possibly prevail in this lawsuit," the company said, arguing that its Joe Camel campaign was aimed only at adult smokers. "It does not and never has had any other objective."
Reynolds said "No matter how much our critics wish it were the case, Joe Camel is not a factor in underage smoking," Reynolds said.
